rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the disbelievers’ fate, the passage portrays the believers’ reward, highlighting blessings the affluent had treated as signs of superiority.
rows.anchor: After referring to the fate of the disbelievers, these verses depict the fate of those who professed belief in the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Descriptions of Paradise and Hell belong to the mutashābihāt: parables make the unseen intelligible, while God alone knows their actual form.
rows.anchor: the details of Paradise and Hell that they are among the mutashābihāt. Through such parables and similes, the details of the unknown world are made comprehensible to us.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic descriptions use what Arabs know and value, since a parable works only when its audience understands its purport.
rows.anchor: only those parables and similes can be effective if the addressee knows their purport.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-person parable exposes opponents who take worldly success as proof of their beliefs, infer that the afterlife is imaginary, or expect to fare better there than believers.
rows.anchor: they regarded their worldly success to be proof of the veracity of their ideology and deeds; when Muslims would warn them of God and the Hereafter, they would reply that since they were better off than them in worldly affairs

none: English translation of the verses only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable mirrors Quraysh’s outward and inward arrogance and the conflict between truth and falsehood; the poor companion has faith and joy in knowing God despite lacking orchards.
rows.anchor: The arrogant among the Quraysh are narrated a parable here which mirrors their inner and outer selves and also makes them see the fate of the conflict between truth and falsehood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving the affluent man two orchards rather than one signifies the completion of God’s favour, as do the two gardens promised in al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: The fact that one of them was given two and not one orchard is to express the completion of favour on him by God. In S ūrah al-Ra ḥmān too it is mentioned that the dwellers of Paradise will be given two orchards.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ideal Arab orchard had grapes, fruit-bearing date palms for beauty and shelter from hot winds, seasonal farmland, and a central stream with tributaries watering it.
rows.anchor: For the Arabs, the concept of an ideal orchard was one which was of grapes; its borders have date-palms that bear fruit, enhance the splendour of the orchard and protect it from sizzling winds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two orchards so richly provided leave a person with little else to desire in worldly life.
rows.anchor: What else can a person need in this world if he has not one but two such orchards!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard owner should have responded to God’s favour with gratitude, but instead argued when his companion urged gratitude and warned of divine wrath for ingratitude.
rows.anchor: what should have been expected from him was an expression of immense gratitude to the God Who blessed him with this favour. However, what actually happened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for its fruit indicates that the exchange occurred when the crop was ready for harvest, when affluence especially intoxicates an orchard owner.
rows.anchor: when the crops were ready for harvesting. Obviously, on such occasions, the owner of an orchard becomes all the more inebriated with his affluence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard owner entered while voicing his claims in a state of pride and arrogance over his wealth.
rows.anchor: he entered the orchard and uttered the words stated in the verse while he was expressing pride and arrogance on his affluence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle in the verse separates the two objects of the verb as an auxiliary element, a usage found in classical Arabic and other languages.
rows.anchor: It is not directly related to the sentence. Examples of such auxiliary usage can be seen in classical Arabic literature as well as in our own languages.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains the words for the calamity and barren land as thunder and hail, and land totally devoid of vegetation.
rows.anchor: the land which is totally barren and devoid of any vegetation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer warns his arrogant companion that haughtiness could bring this calamity upon the orchard.
rows.anchor: Here the believer is informing his arrogant companion of a likely consequence of his haughtiness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about water going into the ground means it sinks completely; even without hail, losing the stream would leave the orchard owner helpless.
rows.anchor: In other words, instead of thunder and hail visiting them even if the running stream that waters their orchard disappears in the land, what could they or anyone else do anything?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant become so absorbed in comfort that they cannot imagine ruin breaching their defenses, yet God can raze them in a moment.
rows.anchor: All the arrogant and haughty people of this world have the same mentality. They become so engrossed in their luxuries and comforts that it weighs down heavily on them to even think that this lavishness can ever see its doom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard is destroyed by a sudden calamity; its fences collapse and the owner wakes to the ruin he had thought impossible.
rows.anchor: Finally, the orchard reached the same fate with which the believer had warned his companion. An earthly or heavenly calamity decimated it in the blink of an eye.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wish not to associate partners means he regrets arrogance that treated the orchard as his own achievement and entitlement; he should have seen it as God’s gift and been grateful.
rows.anchor: it was a gift of God and he should have been greateful for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The group whose numbers and strength the orchard owner boasted about did not come to his rescue when disaster struck.
rows.anchor: when the calamity destroyed the orchard, the group he was proud never came to him rescue.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also lacked the strength to retaliate on his own.
rows.anchor: Moreover, he himself also did not have the strength to take revenge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word hinnālika points to the time when God’s punishment is manifested in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: points to the time of manifestation of God’s punishment in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names the righteous’ fate because wrongdoers’ fate was already given; rewarding the righteous is the real purpose, while punishing wrongdoers is its necessary consequence.
rows.anchor: The verse only mentions the fate of the righteous because the fate of the wrongdoers has already been mentioned earlier. It may be kept in mind that whether it is the punishment of this world or of the next, the real purpose is to reward the righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next parable addresses people blinded by love of worldly life: its ornaments will not accompany them to the next world; only righteous deeds endure as what they can earn.
rows.anchor: none of the adornments of this world will go with them to the next world. Only their righteous deeds will. So anyone who has to earn anything should do righteous deeds.

none: Verse text and translation heading only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly allure blinds the affluent as they become entangled in material pursuits.
rows.anchor: It is these lures that make the affluent close their eyes as they get entangled in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥadīd explains the parable as worldly amusement, adornment, and competition in wealth and children; its luxuriant growth lures disbelievers before withering.
rows.anchor: Know that the parable of the life of this world – a sport and an entertainment and an embellishment and in the matter of wealth and children a mutual show off and a quest to outdo one another in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affluent are so captivated by luxury, possessions, status, and comfort that they make no time for anything else.
rows.anchor: Except for luxury and comfort, cinema and theatre, cars and houses, wealth and assets, money and bank accounts, status and position nothing carries weight in their eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly luxuriance is temporary: rain first creates it, but it soon withers, and God has power both to produce and to decay it.
rows.anchor: Rain does temporarily create luxuriance. Yet, not far away is the time when it will whither away. God has power over all things.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabia, tribal and family backing made children a source of strength, and people displayed their numbers in gatherings to assert superiority.
rows.anchor: in Arabia, the defence and power of a person depended on familial and tribal support, his strength depended on an abundance of children.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person should place hope in lasting righteous deeds, which bring eternal blessings.
rows.anchor: The verse states that if a person has to pin hopes on it should be righteous deeds. They will reap eternal blessings for him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth now looks lush, adorned by mountains, forts, gardens, and orchards, but God will strip away these adornments and gather everyone, without exception or worldly distinction.
rows.anchor: a day will come when even these mountains shall be uprooted, what to speak of other things and the land will become bare and barren. The earth will be stripped of all its adornments.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before God, people will stand helpless like slaves, deprived of guards, attendants, and the assets they once boasted about because they never expected accountability.
rows.anchor: they will appear before their like slaves with hands tied; neither will they have their battalion of guards and attendants about them nor the assets they proudly boasted about

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The register is the record of people’s deeds; its detailed preservation ensures that God wrongs no one and each receives what they earned.
rows.anchor: here means the register of deeds of people. All the elaborate arrangement mentioned in the verse for recording deeds would be because God does not want to be unjust to anyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are warned that they follow Satan’s denial and take him and his progeny as protectors and objects of worship, despite his declared enmity toward Adam’s descendants.
rows.anchor: they have followed the footsteps of Satan in their attitude of denial. They regard him to be their real help and support and worship him and his progeny.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an mercifully presents truth in varied ways, yet its opponents insist on torment and scourge instead of accepting mercy.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān that is being read out to them is a great mercy for them. It is presenting before them the reality in various styles so that they can truly appreciate it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhū al-Qarnayn humbly credits his barrier to his Lord’s blessing, unlike Quraysh leaders who boast of lasting feats; he says the wall will fall when God’s promise arrives.
rows.anchor: Dhū al-Qarnayn did not express any arrogance. He did not say like these haughty leaders of the Quraysh that he had accomplished a feat that will be an abiding one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard owner arrogantly thought his lush garden indestructible, while Dhū al-Qarnayn is the grateful servant who credits his achievement to God and remembers God’s certain promise.
rows.anchor: the mentality of one of them was inflicted with arrogance: when he entered enter his lush orchard, he would haughtily say that he does not think that it will ever be destroyed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Connecting the gathering verse to Dhū al-Qarnayn’s final statement about God’s promise, the author reads it as further signs of the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: By connecting this verse to the statement of Dhū al-Qarnayn mentioned in the last verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse points to the disappearance of boundaries between seas and mountains and to nations colliding like waves.
rows.anchor: the borders between seas and mountains will all go away one day and nations will crash into one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says science has already removed some barriers, while whatever remains will also lose meaning near Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: Science has already gotten rid of the barriers between the seas and mountains; however

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who are blind to the warning cannot foresee Hell now, but will see it with their own eyes on that day.
rows.anchor: today these intellectually blind people do not foresee Hell but on that day they will see it with their very eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are so intellectually deprived that prophetic reminders cannot awaken them and they cannot bear God’s warnings.
rows.anchor: so intellectually deprived were these people that none of the prophetic reminders could open their eyes and when God’s warnings were sounded to them, they could not bear them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse delivers a warning to the wretched people who rely on other guardians besides God.
rows.anchor: A warning is sounded to these wretched people in this verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses humble people who thought themselves superior and mocked revelation: they will become insignificant and taste Hell as the consequence.
rows.anchor: Today they regard themselves to be superior but on the Day of Judgement they will become insignificant. They haughtily made fun of God’s revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who accepted faith and did righteous deeds receive the lasting hospitality of Paradise.
rows.anchor: This verse states the reward of those who accepted faith and did righteous deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are manifestations of God’s power and wisdom found within human beings and throughout the world.
rows.anchor: refers to the signs of God’s power and wisdom found scattered within human beings as well as outside them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea-as-ink image answers those mocking the Qur’an and demanding a miracle: God’s signs cannot be exhausted, though only perceptive people see them.
rows.anchor: This verse is a response to the arrogant who would make fun of the Qur’ ān and demand a miracle to be shown to them. In S ūrah Luqmān, an even stronger response is given.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should tell them that signs are God’s prerogative: he only recites revelation, never claimed divinity, and need not satisfy their demand for a miracle.
rows.anchor: He is only God’s envy who recites divine revelations that He sends to him. The Prophet (sws) should tell them that he has never claimed to be God so that he should fulfil their demand of showing a miracle.
